summary:
Puducherry is a union territory of India with a partial legislature. Legal recognition of gender identity, identity-document rules and welfare policy for transgender people are set principally by the central government in New Delhi, and no Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file. The framework a visitor meets in Puducherry is therefore the national one.

That framework was rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which amends the 2019 law by removing the right to self-identification, narrowing the statutory definition of transgender person, and limiting legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. The bill also mandates medical certification as a condition of identity recognition. Both houses approved the measure and it awaited presidential assent as of the most recent reporting.

Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a major reversal of the rights affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling and has urged the president not to sign it. The government's stated case is that the narrower definition improves the delivery of welfare schemes. Critics counter that the exclusion catches trans men, trans women and non-binary and gender-fluid people who identify outside the recognised categories, and that compulsory medical certification is an attack on privacy and dignity.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and the same court has held that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity falls within the Article 15 prohibition of discrimination by sex. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people interviewed for reporting expressed fear of a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel even though she presented her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have described degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans flowing from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Care access is set at the level of Indian states and the centre rather than by Puducherry. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and in April 2019 the Madras High Court ordered the Tamil Nadu government to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Two assessments of the same national picture point in opposite directions. The United Kingdom's December 2025 policy note treats police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and non-systemic, concentrated in conservative rural areas; the June 2024 victim interviews document abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. A visitor weighing these against the specific incidents at airports and railway stations should read the general assessment and the incident record as measuring different things.

State-level provision in India does not run evenly. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha maintain transgender welfare boards delivering housing subsidies, surgery and pensions, and several states give hijras targeted benefits. Puducherry sits alongside Tamil Nadu, where the Madras High Court issued the sweeping LGBTQIA+ protection guidelines of 7 June 2021 and, in April 2019, ordered an end to sex-selective surgery on intersex infants; how far that machinery reaches into Puducherry is not established by these sources.

Bans on conversion therapy issued by the Madras High Court in 2021 and by the National Medical Commission in 2022 sit alongside clandestine networks that continue to operate, so a prohibition on paper has not ended the practice.

The March 2026 amendment is contested at the point of enactment rather than settled: Human Rights Watch urges the president not to sign it, the government defends it as widening access to welfare, and critics describe it as an attack on the right to exist.

Trans men, trans women and non-binary or gender-fluid residents who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition route, and activists including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist.

Welfare delivery runs through central schemes and state boards. The Ayushman Bharat scheme, expanded in April 2024, covers transition-related healthcare for members of the transgender community, and the Ministry of Finance confirmed in August 2024 that LGBTQ people may open joint bank accounts and name partners as beneficiaries without restriction.

Residents of neighbouring Tamil Nadu can access a transgender welfare board coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, a structure that Puducherry residents do not have on file as running locally.

Intersex residents born in the region carry the documented history of non-consensual assignment surgery; the Madras High Court's April 2019 order directed the Tamil Nadu government to stop sex-selective operations on intersex infants.

Police sensitisation, protection guidelines and the ban on conversion therapy issued in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police on 7 June 2021 are the operative protective machinery for LGBTQIA+ residents in the jurisdiction covered by that judgment, alongside the National Medical Commission's 2022 prohibition.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Puducherry-specific statute, enforcement record, welfare board or incident series appears in the sources; the assessment rests on the national framework and on incidents recorded elsewhere in India.

Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill had received presidential assent at the time of writing is unresolved. Human Rights Watch's appeal of 26 March 2026 was addressed to the president before signature, and later status is not sourced.

The reach of the Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 guidelines and its April 2019 intersex-surgery order into Puducherry is not sourced here, and neither is the presence or absence of a Puducherry welfare board for transgender people.

Police conduct inside Puducherry itself is not sourced. The divergent UK and victim-interview assessments describe India generally, and the individual incidents occurred in Chennai, Kolkata and Assam.

Whether the Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 is administered in Puducherry on the same terms as in the states named is not established by these sources.
